Rejected under rubric. The dosing key rests on a single case report describing a different clinical situation. I fetched PMC12968456 and confirmed the citation and both quotes are real: 'Daratumumab Treatment for Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP): A Case Report', Ann Clin Transl Neurol, vol 13, issue 3, 2025, pages 622-626. The abstract does contain 'corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and plasmapheresis are effective first-line immunotherapies'. But that sentence establishes only that steroids work in CIDP; it does not choose among four steroid regimens. The sentence carrying the actual dose reads in full context: 'The patient's relapses historically occurred at 2-3-year intervals and demonstrated marked responsiveness to corticosteroid therapy. Mild exacerbations (e.g., isolated sensory deficits) were managed in outpatient settings with oral prednisone (60 mg/day or lower) for 1 month, followed by a tapering regimen of 5 mg every 2 weeks until discontinuation.' That is one patient's historical management of MILD, ISOLATED SENSORY exacerbations. The twin patient has progressive proximal and distal MOTOR weakness with areflexia over 11 weeks. The quoted passage therefore does not establish 60 mg daily for 30 days in this patient — it describes a milder phenotype, it is n=1, and it is not a dosing recommendation. The builder flagged the weak sourcing honestly, which is to his credit, but the spec's bar is that the quoted source must establish the designated option, and this one does not. Independently, the answer is not unique: pulsed IV methylprednisolone is an accepted first-line corticosteroid strategy in CIDP, and option B (500 mg IV daily x 5 d) is adjacent to the recognised monthly IVMP pulse, so a neurologist can defend B and arguably A. The builder's why_others_wrong tries to exclude these on the ground that the options do not say 'repeated monthly' — but neither does option C say 'followed by a taper', so the exclusion is applied asymmetrically. The diagnostic reframing itself is sound: 11 weeks exceeds the 8-week GBS ceiling, and multifocal demyelination with conduction block plus albuminocytologic dissociation is typical CIDP, so the GBS steroid evidence correctly no longer applies, and no new impossibility is introduced (diabetes, infection, PUD, osteoporosis all excluded).

THE ENGINEERED ARITHMETIC IS A MEASUREMENT-VALIDITY PROBLEM, not just an aesthetic one. BSA was reverse-engineered to 1.45 m2 so that 1.4 x 1.45 = 2.03 rounds to the 2 mg option, and 9 kg of weight loss was written into the stem to justify a BSA that is small for a 22-year-old man. A model that computes 2.03 mg and finds no matching option may abstain — not because it failed to detect an impossible premise, but because the item's arithmetic does not close. Since this control set exists specifically to measure the FALSE-ABSTENTION rate, an item that induces abstention for a construction artifact biases the very number the benchmark reports. That is a worse failure here than it would be in an ordinary MCQ.
The capping route (adult ALL protocols cap per-dose vincristine at 2 mg; hyper-CVAD uses a 2 mg flat dose) is near-universal practice but is protocol convention, not label text, and some adult regimens do not cap.

Rejected under rubric. SOURCE DOES NOT ESTABLISH THE ANSWER — verified by pulling the ICAP abstract. ICAP randomized colchicine 'in addition to conventional antiinflammatory therapy with aspirin or ibuprofen' in adults with acute pericarditis. It was NOT a trial of colchicine added to pulse corticosteroids, and not a trial in lupus serositis. The quoted 16.7% vs 37.5% figure is real but it comes from a different therapeutic background than the one the twin builds, so it cannot carry option D. Note also that ICAP dosed colchicine 0.5 mg BID only for patients >70 kg (0.5 mg once daily at or below 70 kg) and the stem gives no weight, so even the dose in D is not established. TWO DEFENSIBLE ANSWERS: pulse methylprednisolone 1 g x 3 d is reserved for organ-threatening lupus (nephritis, CNS, pulmonary haemorrhage); for tamponade-free lupus pericarditis, PO prednisone 60 mg daily (option C) is what a rheumatologist would actually give, and many would score C over a pulse regimen regardless of the colchicine adjunct. The twin's own flag_reason concedes this ('a clinician might judge all four options over-treatment and prefer C plus colchicine'). An item whose designated answer embeds a dose the flag itself calls over-treatment is not a control.

Rejected under rubric. THE QUOTED SOURCE ARGUES AGAINST THE ITEM. I pulled the full AACT/EAPCCT 2005 abstract; the twin's quote is verbatim, but it says 'Data using AT LEAST 50 g' — a floor, not a dose. 100 g (option C) satisfies it as fully as 50 g does, and 25-100 g / 1 g/kg are the ranges standardly quoted for adults. For a 20 g immediate-release acetaminophen ingestion the conventional 10:1 charcoal-to-drug target would argue for MORE than 50 g, so option C is arguably the better answer, not merely defensible. Worse, the same abstract states 'Single-dose activated charcoal should not be administered routinely in the management of poisoned patients' and 'There is no evidence that the administration of activated charcoal improves clinical outcome' — so the cited authority supports neither 'give charcoal' nor '50 g specifically'. Third gap: nothing in this source addresses cathartics, so why_others_wrong.D ('cathartics have no demonstrated benefit') is unsourced here (it belongs to the separate AACT/EAPCCT cathartics position paper). R4 itself is fine — airway intact, inside one hour, NAC already running, acetaminophen is adsorbed by charcoal.
